lines.note: Hatsuhatsu or hatsuhatsu na koto denotes something only just adequate. The reduplication is not the first-fruits sense of hatsu found in nearby entries.

runs.text: que eſcaſamente quadra, vem juſta, ou que

lines.note: The Portuguese describes something that barely fits or comes out just right. Quadra concerns suitability here, not a square shape.

runs.text: por poucas não preſtara, ou não ſeruira pe-

lines.note: It nearly would not be useful or serve any purpose. The negative construction explains the narrow margin of adequacy rather than declaring the object wholly useless.
Completes pera nada from the preceding row. This short fragment belongs to the adequacy definition, not the following hatsugan cross-reference.
Hatsugan refers back to hatsu and its example of the first wild birds taken. The reference instruction is italic while Fatçu is Roman in this occurrence.
Hatsumono is the first produce of anything. Vide continues into the Japanese cross-reference on the next physical row.
This is the referenced hatsu, not a new headword. The word is visibly italic here, so its typography is retained independently of the Roman occurrence two rows above.

runs.text: A prima voz do paſſaro na prima

lines.note: Hatsune means a bird's first song of the season. Prima modifies voice, while the second prima continues into primavera across the row boundary.

runs.text: vera como do roxinol, ou gallinha do mato,

lines.note: Completes primavera and gives birds as examples. Roxinol is the Portuguese nightingale designation; it should not be used to force a modern zoological identification of every Japanese bird in the entry.
Hototogisu is the Japanese cuckoo name embedded in italic Portuguese; the scan supports its italic treatment. The new example starts hatsune wo dasu, producing the first seasonal song.

runs.text: Cantarem a primeira vez os paſſaros

lines.note: Wo dasu completes hatsune wo dasu from the preceding row. The Portuguese plural birds supplies the subject of singing for the first time.
The first song is located in spring or summer. The printed two-word prima vera is preserved rather than standardized.

Hatsuki is the eighth lunar month, glossed by the printed Fachiguachi. Although modern hachigatsu is familiar, the visible final chi is retained; the Portuguese eighth moon confirms the calendrical meaning.
Hatsutorigari or hatsutogari is the first outing for falconry. The shorter alternative is explicitly printed, not an accidental omission of ri in this transcription.

runs.text: meira vez à caça do falcão.

lines.note: Completes the first hunting excursion with a falcon. The register label P. and its period are Roman, distinct from the preceding italic explanation.
Hatsuo is defined broadly as first produce or first fruit. It should not be replaced by the familiar fish word katsuo merely because the sound sequence looks similar.
Completes fruita primera. The printed primera lacks the additional i of modern primeira and is preserved as a local spelling.

runs.text: Certo liuro de verſos, ou utas

lines.note: The title is associated with Hachidaishū, the eight major poetry collections. Utas is Japanese uta with a Portuguese plural ending, and its final s is short in the scan. The headword's worn accent is retained as transcribed rather than inferred from the modern title.
Completes the identification of the verses as Japanese. The previous row's utas is therefore poetry terminology inside the Portuguese description, not an independent dictionary entry.
The compound denotes hurried activity or movement. The Portuguese reflexive verbs make this an action or state, not a place name resembling hattō.
Fatdô suru supplies the verbal construction for that hurried activity. Suru is ordinary Japanese here and is not a grammatical abbreviation.
Hateru means coming to an end. The abbreviated historical inflection should not be expanded by simply concatenating every printed ending without accounting for stem replacement.
Nō ga hateta says the dramatic performance ended. Auto denotes the play here; the item marker introduces another sense of hateru on the following row.
To die is the further sense of hateru. This one-word definition belongs to the verb above, not the noun hate that follows.
Hate is the end or limit, now a noun. Cabo and fim are synonymous in this context, not a rope or geographical cape.
Hatekuchi is the beginning or cause of destruction. Kuchi can mark an opening or point of origin; the compound is not interpreted literally as an anatomical mouth.
Completes destruição de alguma coisa, the destruction of something. The cedilla and nasal ending belong to the split Portuguese noun.

runs.text: Remate, ou cabo de algũa couſa.

lines.note: Hateha denotes the conclusion or final end of something. The transmitted fa belongs to the native word and is not a Portuguese abbreviation.
Hatei is wave-bottom, glossed component by component as nami and soko. The scan supports long s in ſoco, and Portuguese beneath the waves excludes hoko or foco here.
Hatei ni shizumu means sinking below the waves. Fundir-se has the sinking sense here, not necessarily melting a material.
Completes the waves phrase; S. is a register label. It is not an additional Japanese word to feed to the kana converter.
Hateshi is an end or limit. The pairing fim/termo gives the nominal sense rather than the verb hatasu discussed on the previous page.

The dictionary prefers the fuller hachijiku form to the compressed headword, referring to eight scrolls. Gi represents ji here; the preferred Japanese form is visibly italic within the explanatory sentence.

The eight divisions belong to the Lotus Sutra, Hokekyō. The scan shows the title in Roman with a final marked o; its worn caron is consistent with the title's established spelling, not an unmarked modernizing replacement.
Hatsugen is explained as kotoba wo okosu, beginning to speak. The printed absence of a separating period after the headword is retained rather than supplied from NINJAL's normalized entry boundary.

runs.text: meçar a falar. ¶ Itẽ, Palauras altiuas, ou de

lines.note: Completes começar and adds lofty or boastful speech as another sense. The item distinction matters: not every act of beginning to speak is boasting.
Hatsugen wo hanasu illustrates uttering such boastful words. Fanfarrice supplies the pejorative sense and the final Di- continues into dizer.
Completes dizer semelhantes palavras, saying words of that kind. This closes the boasting example, not the forthcoming intelligence definition.
Hatsumei is clarity of intelligence, chie no akiraka na koto. The older sense is intellectual brilliance, not simply the modern noun invention.

runs.text: tendimento claro, & agudo como de Anjo, ou

lines.note: Completes entendimento and compares a clear, sharp mind to an angel's. The comparison reflects the Portuguese explanatory frame, not an additional Japanese religious term.

runs.text: homem muito raro em letras, & ſaber. Vt,

lines.note: Alternatively the comparison is an exceptionally learned person. Raro means outstanding or uncommon in learning, not someone who seldom reads.
Hatsumei na hito is such a brilliant or learned person. The attributive na makes the construction grammatical and is not part of the noun hito.
Knowledge completes the preceding person's accomplishments. This short row remains part of the hatsumei example.
Hatsumō is glossed by kamige, hair of the head. This nominal hair sense must not be replaced by the modern growth-of-hair interpretation solely from familiar kanji.
Hatō denotes waves, with nami repeated as the component glosses. The new example starts the same noun followed on the next row by wo tatamu.
Hatō wo tatamu describes waves piling over one another. Tatamu has the layering sense rather than literally folding an object by hand.
Completes the piling of waves one upon another; encapelar-se likewise describes rising or heaping seas. The printed nasal abbreviation is retained.
This hatō is glossed as waves and islands, nami and shima, distinct from the preceding column's repeated wave gloss. The Portuguese explicitly includes islands.
Hatō wo shinogu means traversing seas and islands with difficulty. Shinogu supplies the overcoming or enduring sense rather than a neutral sightseeing journey.
With hardship completes the travel example. Trabalho denotes difficulty here, not employment or a separate work-related entry.
Hato is pigeon or dove. The Portuguese feminine and masculine forms are alternatives for the bird, not two Japanese headwords.

runs.text: Cais, ou lugar acommodado pera deſ-

lines.note: The homonymous hato is a wharf or suitable landing place. This geographical sense is distinguished from the bird by cais and the following disembarking verb.
Completes desembarcar. The Roman X. is the regional usage label, not a Japanese abbreviation; its period shares the Roman treatment.
Abumi no hatomune is the protruding front or breast of a Japanese stirrup. Pei continues into peito; the compound's pigeon-breast imagery explains the shape.

runs.text: to do estribo de Iapão. ¶ Itẽ,

lines.note: Completes the stirrup definition, then repeats hatomune for a human chest shape. The item marker keeps these two related senses apart.

runs.text: Peito alto, & ſaido a fora de homem.

lines.note: A raised, outward-projecting chest of a person is the second sense. Saido a fora describes protrusion, not a person physically leaving a place.
The compressed spelling redirects to Fappǒ, happō. The printed t before p is kept rather than replaced by the preferred spelling inside the headword itself.

The dictionary prefers Facqẽ to Fatqen for religious colleagues of the same origin or affiliation. Latin potius is italic instructional text, not Japanese; the nasal abbreviation in the preferred form is visibly printed.
The colleagues share the same country, sect, or school. This is an affiliation definition, not merely all Buddhist clergy indiscriminately.
Hakkō is equated with happō, the eight directions or quarters. Potius again introduces the preferred spelling and is italic; the Japanese alternatives remain Roman.
Completes the eight parts of the world, meaning the directional quarters. The short row belongs to the preceding numerical definition.

runs.text: Pòs de farinha de arroz, ou de ceuada

lines.note: Hattai is powdered rice or barley flour. The following torrada qualifies the roasted grain preparation, not a verb describing consumption.
Roasted completes the preparation description. The single word is part of the food entry and should not be attached to the following mushroom definition.

runs.text: Hũa eſpecie de cugumelos que ſe co-

lines.note: Hattake is a mushroom eaten in Japan. The spelling cugumelos is retained; no precise species is imposed from the name alone.
Completes comem, are eaten, and identifies Japan as the place of use. This is a continuation, not an imperative to eat mushrooms.
Hatta to is an adverb meaning suddenly. Adu. labels the part of speech and is italic with the Portuguese definition.
Hatta to akireta describes sudden astonishment. Historical akireru here means being struck with amazement, rather than only the modern sense of exasperation.

runs.text: Cruz ẽ q̃ crucificão ao modo de Iapão.

lines.note: Hattsuke names the cross or execution frame used for Japanese-style crucifixion. The dictionary defines the apparatus here, not just the act of punishment.

runs.text: Oito ceos de que ſe tra-

lines.note: Hatten is explicitly explained as yatsu no ten, eight heavens. The Portuguese continues into the Buddhist context on the next row.
Buppō is the Buddhist teaching within which these heavens are discussed; the scan has Roman Buppô inside the Portuguese. Item then begins a different sense involving small marks.

runs.text: ou riſcas que ſe poem no principio dalgũa eſcri-

lines.note: These are dots or strokes placed at the beginning of a writing. The split escritura is Portuguese, not a Japanese technical term.

runs.text: tura como ſinaes que o diabo teme.

lines.note: The marks are described as signs feared by the devil. This is the missionaries' explanatory framing of protective signs, not a neutral identification of a particular deity.
Hatto, glossed nori, means laws and ordinances. The scan's initial L and Portuguese legal sense both support Leis, not the former Deis.

runs.text: Montinho de pedras, como tumulo que

lines.note: This hattō is a small mound of stones serving as a tomb monument. Its long vowel distinguishes it from the preceding legal hatto.

runs.text: fazem ſobre as couas dos defuntos.

lines.note: The stone mound is made over the graves of the dead. Covas are burial pits in this context, not caves inhabited by living people.

Another hattō denotes a raised place like a pulpit. The o-mark is extremely faint in the scan; the existing caron is retained provisionally, and NINJAL also flags the original's unclear open/closed marking for this entry.

runs.text: Certo Dôbucu ſingello que ſe veste

lines.note: Hattoku is an unlined dōbuku outer garment. The embedded Japanese garment name is italic here, with a visible circumflex rather than a Portuguese nasal tilde.
It is worn over another garment. Singello in the previous row refers to a single or unlined layer, not necessarily a poor-quality garment.
Faua is the historical hawa form for mother. It is not mechanically modernized to haha merely because that is the familiar modern form.
Hahago means the same, mother, when speaking respectfully. The explicit fa-fa spelling contrasts with Faua above and should not be leveled to it.
Respect completes the honorific qualification. This is usage information for hahago, not an independent translation of a new Japanese item.
Hawagimi is an honorific mother expression, reflected in senhora mãe. Guimi represents gimi with hard g before i, unlike gi alone.
Hawake no kaze denotes a wind passing over vegetation; the expression should not be connected with the nearby mother words merely by spelling. The usage label P. is Roman in the scan.

runs.text: que vai paſſando por cima de muitas eruas.

lines.note: The wind passes over many plants or grasses. Ervas supplies the foliage context for hawake, rather than an abstract emotional meaning.
Hawaku means sweeping. The historical wa sequence is retained and should not be normalized to modern haku during diplomatic transcription.

runs.text: Sinal como hũa erua, ou flor q̃

lines.note: Hawakimono is a plant- or flower-like emblem. It is not a broom despite its proximity to the sweeping verb.
The emblem is painted on clothing. This completes the visual-design sense and explains why a plant or flower is mentioned.
Hawa oya again means mother, with oya identifying the parental relation. Initial vo represents o here; it should not be read as a European v consonant.

runs.text: Abano redõdo de q̃ vſão nos autos

lines.note: Ha-uchiwa is a round feather fan used in dramatic performances. Autos means plays in this context, not vehicles or documents.

runs.text: feito de penas de Aguia, ou falcão.

lines.note: The fan is made from eagle or falcon feathers. Penas is feathers, not penalties, and agrees with the fan's material description.
Haō is rendered as viceroy by the dictionary. This historical equivalence is preserved rather than replaced with a modern political definition of hegemon.
Haokoshi is a small chisel shaped like a hammer. Escoprosinho is a diminutive tool name, not an adjective describing a person's appearance.

runs.text: com que abrem os dentes da lima.

lines.note: The tool cuts or raises the teeth of a file. Dentes is a tool-surface metaphor, and lima is the file rather than a citrus fruit.
Haoku is a ruined house, glossed yabureta ie. This Sino-Japanese compound is unrelated to the preceding tool despite sharing the initial hao sequence.
